newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore critics often tangle with law.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore critics often tangle with law.

text.p: Recent suits for defamation against opposition Workers' Party members are the latest in a long line of legal battles critics have had with Singapore's ruling People's Action Party (PAP) and government.

Many of Singapore's prominent opposition politicians have faced court fights with the government or leading members of the PAP, which won 81 of the 83 seats in parliament at the last general election on January 2.
Various journalists and non-political figures have also been prosecuted when authorities felt they had crossed legal boundaries.
GOVERNMENT LEADERS DEFEND LEGAL ACTIONS AGAINST OPPONENTS
Many of these cases have involved defamation or charges of contempt of court, which like all legal actions are tried by a judge. There are no juries in Singapore courts.
Opposition politicians and some Western countries have criticised the PAP's use of the courts, particularly defamation suits, against its opponents.
Opposition politicians have never won a major legal battle with PAP members or ministers.
But government leaders defend their use of the law robustly, saying it is essential to maintain good order in society.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's lawyer and PAP parliamentarian K. Shanmugam argues Singapore is right to use defamation laws to uphold the good name of its leaders.
"If you want to ensure integrity and honesty in public life, then there is much to be said for protecting reputations from untruths and slander," Shanmugam told CNN television recently.
Singapore's U.K. High Commissioner, J.Y. Pillay, argued a similar case in the Economist magazine this month.
"Opposition politicians in Singapore regularly find themselves in legal trouble," he said.
"The reason is they often make reckless, defamatory statements...which they are unable to justify in court."
FIRST OPPOSITION MP DISQUALIFIED BY CONVICTION

Veteran Workers' Party leader Joshua Jeyaretnam, who in 1981 became the first opposition member of parliament elected since independence in 1965, argues Singapore's defamation laws should be amended to allow greater freedom of speech.
Jeyaretnam has paid libel damages of more than S$780,000 ($553,000) to former prime minister, now senior minister, Lee Kuan Yew over the years.
His most famous legal battle was in 1986 when he and Workers' Party chairman Wong Hong Toy were charged with making false statements over party accounts.
The two men were sentenced to a month's imprisonment and a fine of Singapore $5,000 (US$3,030) each for the charges.
The conviction disqualified Jeyaretnam from serving in parliament and from standing as a candidate for five years.
Two years later, Jeyaretnam and Wong won an appeal against conviction to the British Privy Council. In February 1994, Singapore's parliament abolished appeals to the Privy Council.
SOLICITOR GENERAL TURNED GOVERNMENT CRITIC DETAINED
Another Workers' Party MP, Francis Seow, came up against Singapore's Internal Security Act (ISA), which allows detention without trial for up to two years.

In May 1988, Seow, a former Solicitor General, was detained under the ISA, accused of conspiring with U.S. diplomats to destabilise the country, a charge he denied. He was freed in July. He was subsequently fined S$379,200 for evading tax.
SINGAPORE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CHIEF FINED FOR DEFAMATION

The next big legal case against an opposition figure climaxed in April 1994 when the secretary-general of the Singapore Democratic Party (SDP), Chee Soon Juan, was fined S$315,000 for defaming PAP MP S. Vasoo and two other parties.

Chee, who was part of a slate challenging one led by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong in a mini-election in 1992, was sued for comments he made about his dismissal from his job as lecturer at the National University of Singapore. He had been accused of misusing research funds for postage, charges he denied.
INTERNATIONAL HERALD TRIBUNE NEWSPAPER FINED

Christopher Lingle, a U.S. academic at the National University of Singapore, and the International Herald Tribune (IHT) newspaper both faced court action in January 1995 for an article about Asian governments by Lingle in October 1994.

They were fined for contempt of court for an article which did not mention Singapore but contained a sentence about "governments ... relying on a compliant judiciary to bankrupt opposition politicians".

Arguing the article could only refer to Singapore, the Attorney-General cited 11 cases where government politicians had sued opposition figures successfully. He said there was no other country where there had been a large number of such cases.
In a separate civil case for libel over the article, the IHT apologised and paid Lee US$213,000 in damages. Lingle was separately ordered to pay US$71,000 in damages.
JEYARETNAM AND TANG FACE 21 DEFAMATION SUITS

The latest legal action concerns comments by Workers' Party politician Tang Liang Hong in the campaign for the last general election on January 2. Jeyaretnam and Tang face 21 suits for defamation from 11 PAP politicians including Goh and Lee.

With the exception of an action filed by Lee and his son before the election, the initial suits arose from Tang accusing PAP leaders of being liars for charging he was "anti-Christian" and a "Chinese Chauvinist". The PAP leaders then sued him for defamation.
More suits followed after Tang was quoted by newspapers commenting on the legal action. Jeyaretnam is accused of defaming the PAP leaders by advertising Tang's comments.
